nutshell: Animal re-identification is conceptually similar to person re-identification but current practice just borrows person-ReID methods wholesale. This paper builds OpenAnimals, an open codebase for animal re-ID, uses it to systematically 'revisit' whether standard person-ReID tricks (from BoT, AGW, SBS, MGN) actually help on animal benchmarks, finds many don't transfer or even hurt, and proposes ARBase, a simple animal-oriented baseline that outperforms all four person-ReID baselines by wide margins.
contributions: OpenAnimals: an open-source codebase (built on FastReID + WildlifeDatasets) that is compatible with person-ReID methods while supporting many animal species in one unified framework.

A systematic ablation-style 'revisiting' of core design tricks from BoT (random erasing, label smoothing, last stride, BNNeck), AGW (non-local attention, GeM pooling, weighted triplet loss), SBS (freeze training, AutoAug, cosine annealing, soft-margin triplet), and MGN (multi-branch part features) on four animal benchmarks (HyenaID, LeopardID, SeaTurtleID, WhaleSharkID) - showing several techniques that help in person-ReID (e.g. random erasing, AGW's three components, freeze training/AutoAug/soft-margin triplet) do not generalize or actively hurt on animals, while others (label smoothing, last stride, BNNeck, cosine annealing, multi-branch parts) do generalize.

ARBase: a simple animal-oriented baseline built from these findings - wider input aspect ratio (e.g. 384x384 instead of person-ReID's typical taller-than-wide crops), IBN (Instance-Batch Normalization) backbone, a multi-branch global+2-part+3-part head, and dropping random erasing/AutoAug - that beats all four person-ReID baselines by 8-14 points of Rank-1 across all four animal benchmarks.
deficiencies: The headline Table 3 comparison is not resolution-controlled: ARBase runs at [384,384] input while the four baselines are shown at their original person-ReID resolutions ([256,128] or [384,128]). The paper's own Table 4 shows that simply switching a baseline like AGW to [384,384] already gains it from 56.36 to 62.73 Rank-1 on HyenaID with zero architecture changes - meaning a real chunk of ARBase's claimed 14.54-point improvement over the 'second best' baseline is attributable to input resolution alone, not the novel animal-oriented design, and the headline table doesn't isolate this.

Component-level ablations (Tables 4-5) are only shown for HyenaID and WhaleSharkID; the ablations for LeopardID and SeaTurtleID are pushed entirely to supplementary material, so half of the four benchmarks used for the paper's central claims can't be checked against the main text.

The revisiting tables (Tables 1-2), which contain the paper's most surprising claims (e.g. random erasing hurts, AGW's components don't generalize), report single-run numbers with no variance - even though a footnote confirms the authors did run 3-seed repeats elsewhere (for the main Table 3 comparison, deferred to supplementary), meaning the infrastructure for variance existed but wasn't applied to the more counterintuitive per-trick claims.

Species coverage is narrow given the paper's own framing around 'species diversity' as a core challenge - only 4 species are tested (hyena, leopard, sea turtle, whale shark), missing the fine-grained-pattern species (e.g. tigers, giraffes) the related-work section cites as motivating prior work, so how well the ARBase recipe generalizes beyond these 4 specific benchmarks is untested.
notable: The single most impactful, cheapest finding in the paper is arguably the input-aspect-ratio fix: switching from person-ReID's conventional taller-than-wide crops to width>=height crops (e.g. 384x384) measurably helps every baseline tested, with no architecture or training changes needed - a nearly free, broadly reusable insight for anyone adapting a person-ReID codebase to a different object category with different natural proportions (not just animals).
